clue.text: Way to bring back food (not strictly for the birds)

definitions.text: Way to bring back food (not strictly for the birds)

parts.words: Way to bring back food (not strictly for the birds)
parts.note: parent birds bring swallowed food back up to feed their chicks, but people can do it too, so it is not only for the birds

explanation.surface: A description of feeding habits, with a joking aside that it is not just for the birds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not strictly for the birds' plays on the idiom 'for the birds' (worthless) while noting that birds really do feed their young this way.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring swallowed food back up into the mouth is the literal meaning of the verb.

clue.text: One fond of a piece of lamb, say

definitions.text: One fond of a piece of lamb, say

parts.words: One fond of a piece of lamb, say
parts.note: Charles Lamb wrote his essays under the pen name Elia, so a lover of one of his pieces is an admirer of Elia

explanation.surface: Someone who enjoys a cut of lamb at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lamb' looks like meat but is the essayist Charles Lamb; a 'piece' is one of his essays, signed Elia.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes a devotee of Lamb's essays, published under the pseudonym Elia.

clue.text: Peacemakers heard to be in experimental stage

parts.note: UN is the United Nations, whose forces keep the peace
a case heard in court has been tried

explanation.surface: Peace negotiators are reported to be only at a trial phase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' suggests a sound-alike, but here it means judged in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not yet tested is still at the trial stage.

clue.text: Piece of packing blown under a bonnet?

definitions.text: Piece of packing blown under a bonnet?

parts.words: Piece of packing blown under a bonnet?
parts.note: a seal between engine parts can fail or 'blow', and a car's bonnet (the British word for the hood) covers the engine

explanation.surface: A bit of packaging material swept beneath somebody's hat.
explanation.walkthrough: A bonnet is a hat but also, in Britain, the hinged cover over a car's engine.
explanation.definitionFit: This seal is a shaped piece of packing that fits between engine surfaces, and a failed one is said to have blown.

clue.text: Tidy clip on ground for the amphibioushardtop

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held: 'Tidy clip on ground for the amphibioushardtop'. TERRA (ground) + PIN (clip) explains the letters, but 'Tidy' has no role and looks garbled; no source gives the printed text.
annotationWithheld.clue: Tidy clip on ground for the amphibioushardtop

clue.text: Optical illusion that is currently popular

indicators.note: an illusion makes things look other than they are, so the letters are seen in a new order

explanation.surface: An optical illusion that happens to be in fashion right now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'illusion' rearranges OPTICAL into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of current interest, in the news, is relevant to the present moment.

clue.text: Though in a car, one can take a jar

definitions.text: Though in a car, one can take a jar

parts.words: Though in a car, one can take a jar
parts.note: a jar here is a jolt, and a car part soaks up jolts, though the surface suggests drinking while driving

explanation.surface: Even in a car you might manage a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'jar' is British slang for a drink, but here it means a jolt from the road.
explanation.definitionFit: This suspension part absorbs jolts from the road surface.

clue.text: Bared tum, prepared for a tattoo

indicators.note: prepared means made ready in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone shows their belly, ready to have a tattoo inked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prepared' rearranges BAREDTUM. A tattoo is also a military drum signal, not just body art.
explanation.definitionFit: A tattoo is a rhythmic signal beaten on a drum, especially to recall soldiers.

clue.text: Intolerant of containerised pieces, perhaps

indicators.note: broken into pieces, so the letters of the word are reassembled differently

explanation.surface: Someone who cannot abide goods shipped in containers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pieces' rearranges CONTAINERISED into the answer; 'perhaps' flags the loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A thoughtless, intolerant person shows no regard for other people.

clue.text: Elevate one in the army

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the other, as the clue's 'in' says

parts.note: a host is an army, as in heavenly host
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Promote a soldier serving in the army.
explanation.walkthrough: HOST is an old word for an army.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise or lift up something is to elevate it.

clue.text: Fight at club leaves metal in a heap

parts.note: a scrap is a fight
an iron is a type of golf club

explanation.surface: A brawl at a nightclub leaves behind a pile of metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'club' suggests a nightclub, but it is a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: Discarded metal waiting to be melted down is piled in junkyards.

clue.text: Simple melody of the French in Spanish bar

indicators.note: the clue's 'in' places one piece inside another

parts.note: a cantina is a bar in Spanish-speaking countries
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A tune of French origin heard in a bar in Spain.
explanation.definitionFit: This musical term names a smooth, lyrical vocal line, a simple song-like melody.

clue.text: Arrived wearing ring and brooch

indicators.note: wearing here means having on next to it, so one piece follows the other

parts.note: came means arrived
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: Someone turns up with a ring and a brooch on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wearing' puts the ring after CAME rather than around it.
explanation.definitionFit: A carved stone in relief is often set as a brooch.

clue.text: Everybody due to go out to see advert

parts.note: all means everybody

indicators.note: to go out of order, so the letters of the word are mixed

explanation.surface: Everyone owed a trip out to see an advertisement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to go out' rearranges DUE as UDE. 'Advert' is not an advertisement but the verb meaning to refer.
explanation.definitionFit: To advert to something is to refer to it, to mention it indirectly.

clue.text: Wodehouse, say, a source of Uncle Remus's tales?

definitions.text: Wodehouse, say, a source of Uncle Remus's tales?

parts.words: Wodehouse, say, a source of Uncle Remus's tales?
parts.note: the name Wodehouse sounds like wood house, and the old storyteller Uncle Remus told his tales in a humble timber hut

explanation.surface: Asks whether the novelist P. G. Wodehouse supplied the Uncle Remus stories.
explanation.walkthrough: Wodehouse is the author, but heard as 'wood house' it describes the hut.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple dwelling built from tree trunks is a wooden house.

clue.text: If retired, senior chaps have positions at lord's

definitions.note: read as those who have positions at Lord's

indicators.note: retired means drawn back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: elders are senior men

explanation.surface: Older men take up stations at the cricket ground if they retire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' reverses the first word. Lord's is a famous London cricket ground; the definition reads as 'those who have positions at Lord's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket players on the non-batting side each stand at a set spot on the field.

clue.text: Having the same tension, is love pick-me-up needed?

parts.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, O
a tonic is a pick-me-up

explanation.surface: Asks whether love needs a boost.
explanation.definitionFit: The scientific term describes muscles or solutions of equal tone or pressure.

clue.text: It can have an extended index, by the way

definitions.text: It can have an extended index, by the way

parts.words: It can have an extended index, by the way
parts.note: an index is a pointing finger, and roadside pointers often show a hand with forefinger extended; by the way means at the roadside

explanation.surface: A remark, mentioned in passing, about a book with a long index.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by the way' looks like an aside but means beside the road.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside post bearing pointers directs travellers.

clue.text: Sticking variety of dressing?

parts.note: a wound dressing that adheres to the skin, though dressing suggests salad or clothes

explanation.surface: Asks about a salad dressing that clings.
explanation.walkthrough: A sticking plaster is the British name for an adhesive bandage.
explanation.definitionFit: An adhesive bandage stuck over a cut is a kind of wound dressing.

clue.text: Shut up these days for a five year term

parts.note: pent means shut up, confined
AD, anno Domini, marks the present era

explanation.surface: Locked away nowadays for a five-year sentence.
explanation.definitionFit: A group or period of five, from the Greek for five.

clue.text: Pleasing in sound makes you funny to the listener

definitions.note: read as a pleasing quality of sound

indicators.note: what the listener hears is a sound-alike

parts.note: you plus funny in the sense of fake, phony

explanation.surface: Something pleasant to hear makes you seem odd to an audience.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny' here means fake or phony.
explanation.definitionFit: The term means agreeable, harmonious quality of sound in words or music.

clue.text: Not fit? Try a continental spa!

parts.note: un is French for a
a well is a spring or spa

explanation.surface: Feeling poorly? Go and take the waters in Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone ill is in poor health.

clue.text: Lariat used in encore at any rodeo

indicators.note: the letters are used within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A rope used during an encore at a rodeo.
explanation.definitionFit: This rope with a noose is a lasso.

clue.text: Can first man in find this kitchen utensil?

parts.note: a tin is a can
in cricket an opener is the first batsman in

explanation.surface: Asks whether the first person to arrive can find a kitchen gadget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first man in' is a cricket opening batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: A gadget for prising open cans is found in a kitchen drawer.

clue.text: Dinar change-that's rock-bottom

indicators.note: change means alter, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A currency change hits the lowest point.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest point of anything is its low point.

clue.text: Roughly sixteen going to church? Poor living!

indicators.note: roughly means not exactly, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: Sixteen-year-olds going to church lead a hard life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' rearranges SIXTEEN into EXISTEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A bare way of life, as in eking out a poor existence, is mere survival.

clue.text: Noise of Paris?

parts.note: French for 'they say', meaning rumour, noised about in Paris

explanation.surface: The din of the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noise' means rumour, as in something noised abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A French phrase used in English for a piece of gossip or hearsay.

clue.text: They set down stretchers on site

definitions.text: They set down stretchers on site

parts.words: They set down stretchers on site
parts.note: a stretcher is a brick laid lengthwise in a wall, not a medical carrier

explanation.surface: Paramedics put down stretchers at the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stretchers' suggests first aid, but builders use the word for bricks laid along a wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Builders set bricks in courses on a building site.
